en: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī:
*Siddhāntabindu* (Now,
the *Siddhāntabindu*)
Introduction: Having prostrated before the Lord of the Universe, the Teacher of the World, the illustrious Śaṅkarācārya, who is a new incarnation [of Śiva].
I make a certain effort for the sake of awakening those who are indolent toward hearing the Vedānta scriptures.

Indeed, here the venerable Śrīmacchaṅkara, desiring to uplift all living beings—both directly and through tradition—composed this *Daśaślokī* in order to briefly awaken them to the Self, whose nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and free, by means of discrimination from that which is not the Self.

Now, it may be objected: everyone in the world perceives the Self, the locus of the "I-notion," as "I am," through discrimination from the non-Self which is the object of the "this-notion," and yet they experience suffering.

If it is argued that the exposition of the true nature of the Self is useless because it would be making known what is already known and because it serves no purpose, we say: no. Since the body, senses, and mind—which are the objects of the notion "this"—are, by their very definition as being illumined by consciousness, perceived through non-discrimination as the objects of the notion "I," there arises, even with respect to the pure Self, the false identification of it with suffering and so forth; therefore, [the teaching is necessary] for the sake of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, which is derived solely from the scripture.
Because that [ignorance] is ceased along with its root, and because it makes known what was previously unknown and serves a purpose, the exposition of the reality of the Self is not futile.
And of that reality of the Self, [it is said]: "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.8.7).
The great Vedāntic mahāvākya, such as "I am Brahman" (BAU I.4.10), alone is the means of valid knowledge.

And since a sentence functions as a communicator only by means of the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words, and because the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*— which are required for the present sentence— are not established through any other source, those two must also be known through the scripture itself.

Consequently, scriptural passages concerning creation and so forth, such as “from which indeed these beings are born, or by which, once born, they live” (TU III.1.1), serve to establish the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the word *tat*; however, passages such as “truth, knowledge, infinite” (TU II.1) establish its indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).

Thus, scriptural passages concerning waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth— such as, "Just as a great fish swims along both banks" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.3.18)— establish the referent of the term *tvam* (the "thou"). These include such texts as, "This person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.3.7),
and "You cannot see the seer of seeing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.4.2).
The above [passages] refer to the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).

Therefore, since the primary literal connection between the pure individual soul (*śuddhajīva*) and Brahman—both of which have been experienced through intermediate sentences—is untenable within sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), their recollection via secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is established.
Furthermore, because the experience of non-conceptual witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is admitted during deep sleep, [the Upanishads] intend to instruct one regarding the non-dual Brahman.

Although words such as "truth" (*satya*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), when employed, have their denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward consciousness qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), they nonetheless bring about the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) specifically regarding that aspect of pure consciousness alone, because their primary purport (*tātparya*) lies in that very [consciousness].
For they maintain that even from words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*), a non-conceptual recollection can arise, since the function of a word is dependent upon its intended purport.
By this, the appearance of both the means of knowledge (*pramiti*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*) in the comprehension of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) is refuted;
for the state of non-cognitive absorption (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*) is established by both Śruti and Smṛti.

Furthermore, because of its being indirect (*pārokṣya*) and dualistic (*sadvitīyatva*), one does not achieve the fulfillment of all goals through the mere experience of the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam* alone.
There is no tautology because the expressed meanings (vācyārtha) appear as distinct;
yet, because the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) is one, it possesses the quality of being an indivisible referent (akhaṇḍārthatā).
Furthermore, it is not contradictory for the memory produced by the words—which conforms to the non-conceptual sentence-meaning—to be itself non-conceptual, just like the direct experience itself.
Furthermore, in the case of the determinate comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, the recollection of the determinate word-meanings is an auxiliary factor;

however, in the present instance, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*), because it alone possesses the capacity to remove ignorance by virtue of being a valid cognition (*pramā*).
Therefore, there is no impossibility of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) occurring without a delimitor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
For the presentation of word-meanings that are conducive to the meaning of the sentence in question is itself accomplished through *śakti* (denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

Now, if it is argued: "In that case, once the presentation of word-meanings and the comprehension of the sentence-meaning have occurred from the Vedānta sentences themselves, and since that [comprehension] possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), how can there be the cessation of ignorance and its effects by means of that [comprehension]?"—is this true?

Although the Vedāntas, by virtue of their intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), produce a non-conceptual direct realization of the Self (*nirvikalpaka-ātmasākṣātkāra*), nevertheless, for those of dull intellect, that [realization] lacks the capacity to destroy ignorance due to the obstruction posed by doubts arising from the conflicting assertions of disputants (*vādi-vipratipatti*).

However, when doubt is removed through inquiry (*vicāra*), the cessation of ignorance occurs without exception; thus, inquiry is commenced for the purpose of refuting the conflicting assertions of disputants which serve as the seed of doubt.
The first section:
Determination of the meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha). Therein, the conflicting views regarding the meaning of the term "thou" are first presented.

Although the referent of the term *tat* (That) is more venerable because it is the primary subject matter of the scripture’s purport, the referent of the term *tvam* (Thou) is even more venerable than that, as it is the one who partakes in liberation, which is the fruit of the scripture.
Regarding this, the Cārvākas hold that the referent of the term *tvam* consists merely of the four elements transformed into the form of the body;
others maintain that it consists of the sense organs, such as the eyes, individually.
Others say they are the "assembled";
some say "mind";
others say "vital breath."
The followers of the Sugata maintain that consciousness is momentary;
the Mādhyamikas hold it to be empty;
and the Digambaras assert that [the self] is distinct from the body and the senses and is of the same dimension as the body.
The Vaiśeṣikas, Tārkikas, and Prābhākaras hold that [the self] is an agent, an enjoyer, insentient, and all-pervading;
the Bhāṭṭas hold that it is insentient and of the nature of consciousness;
and the Sāṅkhyas and Pātañjalas hold that it is solely an enjoyer and of the nature of pure consciousness.

The followers of the Upaniṣads maintain that [the Self], though appearing as an agent and so forth due to ignorance, is in the ultimate sense devoid of all attributes (nirdharmaka) and consists solely of supreme bliss and consciousness.

Thus, when the conscious Self—established by the general notion of "I"—is rendered doubtful by the conflicting views of various disputants, the venerable Teacher speaks in order to determine the specific object of that "I-notion":
"It is not earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space, nor the senses, nor their aggregate."
Because it is non-conclusive, that which is established as one even in deep sleep is the undifferentiated, solitary Śiva; I am He alone. // 1 //
I am the objective support of the notion of "I";
I am one, without a second;
I am undifferentiated, remaining unsublated even when all duality is sublated.

Śiva is of the nature of supreme bliss and consciousness, because he alone is the embodiment of auspiciousness; he is absolute (kevala), devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka); therefore, being non-dual and uncontradicted by any means of valid cognition, supreme bliss-consciousness itself is the objective support of the notion of "I. Thus, the meaning is that the position of the Upaniṣads alone is the most excellent.
In order to establish this, intending to refute the views of other proponents, he first refutes the doctrine that the body is the self with the words: "Neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor space.
In this context, the word "not" (na) is to be connected individually with each term.
One should understand that there is a mutual absence of identity, such that whatever is earth, that is not the "I," and whoever is the "I," that is not earth.
Even though the proponent does not accept the selfhood of each individual element such as earth, since he accepts it only for the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), nevertheless—

given that in his view a whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, that this would entail the acceptance of a fifth principle, and that he does not admit relations such as conjunction because there is no unifier (*saṃhantṛ*)— the aggregate is untenable; with this intention, [the author] refutes the elements individually.

The doctrine that the body is composed of the elements has been refuted. Furthermore, although in the view of those who maintain that the four elements are the ultimate reality, space— which is considered to be a non-existent, stable absence of obstruction— is not the material cause of the body, nevertheless, according to our own established position (siddhānta), it is accepted as being a positive entity (bhāva) because it is admitted to be the material cause of the body.
In that case as well, [the view] is refuted because it would entail the consequence of [the body] being the self.

Alternatively, the refutation of the doctrine that the body is the self extends only up to the words "nor air"; however, the phrase "nor space" refutes the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), because the word *kha* denotes emptiness.
The phrase "nor the sense-faculties" is the refutation of each of the sense-faculties individually being the self.

"Nor is it their collection" means the refutation of the combined elements (*bhūta*) transformed into the form of the body as a whole (*avayavin*), as well as the combined sense-faculties (*indriya*). Previously, the elements were refuted individually without accepting a composite;
now, however, they are refuted even while accepting the composite—this is the distinction.
By the refutation of the primary elements (*bhūta*), there is the refutation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) as being composed of those elements.

By the refutation of the mind, there is the refutation of mental modification (*manovṛtti*)—that is, momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇikavijñāna*) which is distinct from the body and characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth.

This is because, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), knowledge, desire, pleasure, and the like are accepted as having the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as their locus, and because of the Vedic scripture stating, "The mind alone [is the agent] with regard to desire, resolve, and so forth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad I.5.3).

By this, he establishes the thesis that everything from the body up to the mere enjoyer—as asserted by their respective proponents—is non-self (*anātman*). He states the reason for this: "because of its being inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatvāt*), which means because it is variable or perishable.
This is because the Self is unlimited by space and time, whereas limited things like jars and so forth are non-self; furthermore, that which is distinct from space cannot be the Self.

Even though the self is one, the systematic order [of experience] is established by the admission of a difference among the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which are the substrata of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Furthermore, there can be no prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of that [self], because it is contradictory for something to apprehend its own absence; because at the time of the object being apprehended, the subject does not exist; and because at the time the subject exists, the object is absent—[otherwise] there would follow the fallacy of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Moreover, since the self, whose nature is existence, is all-pervasive, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is impossible.
Since duality is established only as having attained identity with the existence of its substratum due to its falsity,
it is impossible for there to be identity between them because it is superimposed like a shell-silver;
therefore, it has that [substratum] as its counter-correlative in terms of being.
And since the body, the sense organs, and so forth are the counter-correlates of non-existence, they do not belong to the Self.

Rather, the secret of the established doctrine is this: although the Self is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness and is non-dual, these [phenomena] are merely indeterminable, being imagined by beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*avidyā*).

An objection might be raised: "Since you accept that the Self is of the nature of consciousness, and since there is an absence of consciousness during deep sleep—as evidenced by the reflection of one who has awakened from sleep, 'I was deeply deluded, I knew nothing'—how can its invariability be established? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Established solely in deep sleep."
This is the meaning:
because the Self is the witness of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it does not cease to exist therein;

otherwise, the subsequent reflection "I was deluded" would be untenable. Even though the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the objects of knowledge (*meya*) are subject to change, the witness of their presence and absence remains unchanging throughout the three periods of time.

If it is argued that the knower (*pramātṛ*), being the locus of valid cognition, is himself the agent and the enjoyer, and like a lamp, is the illuminator of all things—both self and other—and thus does not depend on a witness (*sākṣin*) as objects such as jars do, we say: no.

Because he is subject to modification, it is impossible for him to be the witness of his own modifications; because what is an object of sight cannot be the seer; and because the knower, being subject to transformation, is himself an object of sight.
For only one who is eternally unchanging can be the witness of everything.
If it is argued that a single, immutable, attributeless witness is not accepted because he lacks scriptural authority, we say no.

For [the scriptures declare]: "Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined" (ŚvetU VI.14, MuU II.2.10, KauU II.5.15), and "You cannot see the seer of seeing" (BṛU III.4.2).

For, by the king of the Vedānta authorities, which declares, "The seer is unseen; there is no other seer than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.7.23), that very [Self] has been consecrated as the witness of all.

[Objection: "Is this not a great magical illusion—that the king of valid cognitions (*pramāṇarāja*), setting aside the immutable substrata (*kūṭastha*) which are the locus of valid cognition, instead makes the witness of all (*sarvasākṣin*) the locus of valid cognition?

[Reply: "Certainly; this is indeed a magical illusion, like a dream, because it is a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*). [Objection: "Even so, since the object of perception (*dṛśya*) is insentient (*jaḍa*) like a jar or other objects, how can it be the locus of valid cognition? [Reply: "No;

because, like a mirror or similar surfaces, it possesses extreme transparency (*atisvacchatva*) and thus receives the reflection of consciousness (*cidbimba*), or because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the mind (*citta*)."
If it is asked, "How can there be a reflection of the Self, which is formless and partless?"—
what is the inconsistency here? For the causes of error are manifold.

If it is argued that a reflection belongs only to that which is perceptible by the senses— given that a reflection is observed in crystal and other media even for a hibiscus flower (which has color), and for that which is formless and partless, yet a reflection called an echo is perceived in the case of sound, and because the difference between those two and the commonly accepted [reflections] is established—
[we reply: no, because of the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra).
For even space— which is not perceptible by the senses and is perceived only by a witness— is observed to have reflections in water and other media;
otherwise, there would be no perception of extreme depth even in water that reaches only to the knees.

In that case, why does the perception of a reflection not arise for a blind person in water? [It is because] only that which possesses light and clouds is reflected, and the eye is required for its apprehension.

By this, the positive and negative concomitances regarding the visual organ are explained even in illusions such as "the sky is blue," since in those cases luminous space serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Therefore, it should be understood that only a visual reflection depends upon color-form (*rūpa*).

Nevertheless, if it is asked what the proof is for the reflection of the Self, listen: "In every form He became the counterpart; that is His form for the purpose of being perceived" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad II.5.19), and "By the appearance of Māyā, He makes the Jīva and the Īśvara" (Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya Upaniṣad 9).
“‘It is seen as one and indeed as many, like the moon in water’ (BBU 12), and so forth;
[and] ‘He has entered here’ (BAU I.4.7).”

“Having split open this very boundary, he entered through that door” (AitU I.3.12); “Having emitted that, He entered into that very thing” (TU II.6.1)—the impossibility of explaining such scriptural statements regarding entry otherwise [is established by the Sūtra]: “And [the soul] is merely a reflection” (BS II.3.50).

"Furthermore, the aphorisms of the Great Sage, such as 'And for this very reason, [the soul is] like the reflection of the sun and so forth' (BS III.2.18), serve as the authorities in that regard. And the proponents of the reflection theory (pratibimbavādinaḥ) maintain that this reflection is indeed real."
The proponents of the theory of appearance (ābhāsavādins) maintain that it is indeed false;
however, there is no dispute whatsoever regarding its true nature, which is a separate matter.
Furthermore, its distinction from the insentient is established by scripture as well as by direct experience.
Therefore, it is established that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possesses the status of the knower (pramātṛtva) by means of the superimposition of a reflection.
Now, one might object: even this superimposition (adhyāsa) is not logically possible.
For instance, is the non-self (anātman) superimposed upon the Self (ātman), or is the Self superimposed upon the non-Self?
Not the first, because that [Brahman], being devoid of commonalities and particularities, appearing at all times, and lacking similarity and so forth, cannot possibly be the substratum.
Nor the second, because its falsity is admitted.
For if a false entity were the basis [of cognition], it would follow that one is a proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*);
and if that [false entity] were real, it could not be ceased, which would lead to the consequence of no liberation,
since what is real is never sublated anywhere.
Or [it is] by means of erroneous knowledge as it turns back;
and the Śruti says: "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and one's karmas are exhausted when that Higher and Lower has been seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad II.2.8).
“Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death; there is no other path for the journey” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad III.8);
“The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VII.1.3).
Such passages, demonstrating that the cessation of all saṃsāra results from knowledge, indicate its falsity.
“Only one, without a second” (ChU VI.2.1); “Other than this, everything is perishable” (BAU III.4.2); “There is no diversity whatsoever here” (BAU IV.4.19).
Furthermore, scriptural passages such as, "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad II.3.6), directly establish falsity;
and there is also the inference of falsity based on the quality of being an object of perception, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Furthermore, since the non-self is established only by way of being superimposed upon the Self, there is the superimposition of the Self upon that [non-self];

and since defects, similarity, and so forth are possible for the Self only through the superimposition of the non-self, there is the superimposition of the non-self upon the Self. This also entails the fallacy of circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*) and other such defects.

By this, the claim that "there is no occasion for doubt because the superimposition of the Self and the non-self is constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*)" is refuted, because ignorance itself is untenable in the case of a Self that is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
For instance, is that [nature] superimposed or not superimposed?
In the first case, how could there not be the consequence of faults such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*)?
In the latter case, because it would never be severed, there would be the consequence of no liberation.
Furthermore, if everything were rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*), there would be no distinction between error and valid cognition (*pramā*).

Moreover, it is contradictory for a single self (*ātman*) to possess the nature of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower; or, if one were to accept this lack of contradiction, the Buddhist position would be established.
To this it is replied: First of all, the cognition "I am a human being, an agent, an enjoyer," and so forth, is established for all people.
Furthermore, it is not memory, because it appears as immediate perception and because it is preceded by the non-apprehension of difference [between the self and the body].
Nor is it valid knowledge (*pramā*), because it is sublated by scripture and reasoning.
And thus the Śruti texts declare: "This person consisting of consciousness who is among the vital breaths, the light within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7);
"This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19);
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
“Consciousness, bliss, Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.9.28);
“That Self which is free from evil” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.7.1);
“That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.4.1).
“He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.5.1);
“Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it, for this person is unattached” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.3.15).
Passages such as these demonstrate that the Self is of the nature of a non-agent, a non-enjoyer, and supreme bliss. And this is logical.

Furthermore, that which undergoes modification would result in being non-self due to its being limited; for if it were to apprehend itself by itself, there would be a contradiction between the agent and the object; and because no relation can be established between the seer and the seen, the status of property and property-bearer cannot be maintained either through difference or non-difference. Moreover, on the view that cognition is non-eternal, there is the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in having to admit various individual instances, their mutual differences, destruction, antecedent non-existence, inherence, the universal "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*), and so forth.
Furthermore, because accepting [their] oneness would entail excessive parsimony (*atilāghava*),
for the distinction between cognitions— such as "cognition of a jar" and "cognition of a cloth"— is perceived only by way of the presentation of distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
whereas, by its own nature, cognition is understood to have a single form, namely, "cognition, cognition."

Furthermore, since the cognitions of the arising and destruction of that [object] are also explained by their having as their object a relation with a substrate that must necessarily be postulated; because it is impossible to seize that [objection] as a counter-example, since the cognition of the difference between one jar and another jar occurs quite naturally without reference to any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); and because, if agency and so forth were real, there would follow the consequence of no liberation; and because even space, time, and direction would consequently have to be manifold.
If agency and so forth were real, there would follow the consequence of no liberation.
Furthermore, because the world would fall into total darkness if self-luminosity were not admitted,
and because its nature is bliss due to being the object of supreme love, the Self is indeed of the nature of eternal, self-luminous bliss devoid of attributes; such are the [arguments].
Therefore, since it is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that this is an illusion, some suitable cause for it must also be postulated.

And that which is being postulated is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its substratum (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*) as being superimposed upon itself; thus, it is precisely this indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) ignorance (*ajñāna*) that is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) in the form "I do not know.
Nor is this of the nature of a non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is because it has already been stated that its absence is untenable due to the eternity of knowledge;
furthermore, there would be a logical contradiction arising from the simultaneous presence and absence of the cognition of the locus and the counter-positive.
Nor is it of the nature of a succession of errors, doubts, and their respective latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is immediate, because past, future, error, doubt, and their latent impressions cannot be known as immediate,
and because its nature is that of an obscuration.
And because it produces error and the like;
for the self is changeless,
while the internal organ and so forth are produced by that [self].

And from the scriptural texts concerning its possession of qualities, such as: “The divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3), and “One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10),
and “Indra, through his Māyās, appears in many forms” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
"For they are indeed veiled by untruth" (ChU VIII.3.2);
"enveloped by mist" (TS IV.6.2.2);
and "furthermore, at the end, there is the cessation of all illusion" (SU I.10).

Based on such scriptural passages as these, it is ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone— which is indescribable (*anirvācya*), unreal (*anṛta*), and removable by the knowledge of reality— that is the cause for the superimposition of self and other.
Nor does there follow the fault of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and so forth,
because that is avoided by its being beginningless (*anāditva*).
Because there is no origination due to beginninglessness,
and because the self-luminous Self alone has the nature of that cognition;
therefore, there is the superimposition of ignorance.
The superimposition of the ego (ahaṅkāra) occurs upon consciousness as qualified by that [body];

and upon that [consciousness] as qualified by the ego, there is the superimposition of the attributes of the ego such as desire and volition, as well as the attributes of the senses such as blindness and deafness.

However, it is the established doctrine (siddhānta) that because the senses are themselves beyond direct perception (parokṣa), they cannot be superimposed upon a substrate that is directly perceived (aparokṣa).
And upon that [internal organ] as qualified [by the body], there is the superimposition of the gross body;
its form is "I am a human" by way of attributing a property,
but not a superimposition in its own nature such as "I am the body."
Likewise, because it is perceived as such,
there is the superimposition (adhyāsa) of bodily attributes such as grossness upon that [body];
and upon that [body] thus qualified, there is the superimposition of external attributes such as completeness or deficiency regarding one's son, wife, and so forth.
In this way, there is also the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of consciousness upon [the ego-sense] and so forth, ending with the body, through association (*saṃsarga*).
And due to the gradation in the mediation of this superimposition, there is a gradation in affection.
As it has been said in the *Vārttikāmṛta* (BAUBhV I.4.1031):
"Son is dearer than wealth; the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is dearer than son; likewise, the sense organs are dearer than the funeral cake;
life-breath is dearer than the sense organs; and the Self is dearer than life-breath. Thus it is said.
The *piṇḍa* is the gross body, and *prāṇa* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Furthermore, the fact that the sense organs are dearer than the body is established by experience; for instance, when a shower of weapons or a stream of water falls upon one, it is observed that the eyes are closed.
Therefore, due to this mutual superimposition, superimposition takes the form of a knot between the conscious and the unconscious;
for if one were to accept the superimposition of only one side, it would follow that the other side would not appear,
since it is a rule that only that which is superimposed appears in an error (SS I.36).
Just as in the collective delusion "these are color and silver," there must necessarily be a mutual superimposition (itaretarādhyāsa).
Furthermore, because consciousness remains as the ultimate limit of all sublation, one does not fall into the position of nihilism (śūnyavāda),
since superimposition consists in the appearance of a mixture of the real and the unreal.
Therefore, this successive superimposition of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth is rooted in each preceding superimposition; like a seed and its sprout, it is beginningless (*anādi*).
Furthermore, the superimposition of ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself a single, beginningless entity.

Now, if superimposition is beginningless, how can it be defined as "superimposition is the appearance, in the form of a memory, of something previously perceived elsewhere" (*adhyāsa* = *smṛtirūpaḥ paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsaḥ*)?

If it is argued that by saying this, the commentator contradicts his own statement that [superimposition] is produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) because it has the nature of memory, we say no; for that statement was intended with reference to the superimposition of an effect,
since the definition common to both types [of superimposition] consists merely in "the appearance of one thing in another."

Alternatively, based on the statement of the author of the Commentary, "having coupled the real and the unreal" (BSBh), the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as established in the final doctrine is simply the appearance of a confusion between real and unreal entities.
For this reason, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the definition even in the case of the superimposition of a cause.
Furthermore, since the superimposition of the effect is declared to be beginningless by way of a continuous stream—like that of the seed and the sprout—there is no fault whatsoever.

Thus, once superimposition is established, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as the distinction regarding objects of knowledge and means of knowledge for each respective action, becomes logically consistent even for a single Self.

To explain: the Self, conditioned by ignorance and having attained identity with that ignorance, is called the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī), the Witness (sākṣin), and the Cause of the World, due to the non-discrimination from its own reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa).

The venerable Vārttikakāra states that the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*) and has attained identity with it—is called the agent, the enjoyer, and the knower due to the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between itself and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*).

Furthermore, because the intellects differ in each body, the consciousness that is non-discriminated from them also appears as if divided according to the differences among those reflections of consciousness.

However, since ignorance (*ajñāna*) is undifferentiated everywhere, there is no difference in the reflection of consciousness residing within it; consequently, the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which is non-discriminated from that reflection, never at any time appears as divided.

And in this view, in words such as "That" (tat) and "Thou" (tvam), there is indeed *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication), because the aspect of the denoted meaning—the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) together with its appearance—is abandoned; for even the appearance is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), being distinct from both the insentient and the sentient.
As it is said in the *Saṅkṣepaśārīraka*:
"If, moreover, the word 'Brahman' and likewise the word 'I' denote ignorance along with its appearance..."
In that view, however, the word "I" (ahaṃ) denotes the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and there the indication (lakṣaṇā) is of the type that abandons its primary meaning (jahatī). Thus it is said.

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of co-location (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between bondage and liberation—since bondage belongs only to the reflection (*ābhāsa*) while liberation belongs only to pure consciousness (*kevalacaitanya*)—and that consequently, activity for the sake of one's own destruction would be untenable;
for we accept that pure consciousness itself becomes bound through the medium of the reflection.
As it has been stated by the venerable author of the *Vārttika*:
“For this indeed is our misfortune: the perception of a transmigrating self” (BUBhV).
Therefore, bondage is merely the appearance of pure consciousness, and liberation is its cessation; thus, there is nothing at all inconsistent in this.
Alternatively, consciousness (caitanya) itself, when distinguished from its appearances (ābhāsa), is denoted by terms such as "That" (tat-tva) and so forth.

Since this view does not abandon even a portion of the primary meaning (vācya), it is characterized as *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication that both excludes and includes); thus, there is no defect whatsoever.
This very position is celebrated as the *Ābhāsavāda* (Theory of Appearances).

The authors of the *Vivaraṇa* maintain that the Lord (*īśvara*) is the consciousness of the original image (*bimba-caitanya*) as conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*), whereas the individual soul (*jīva*) is the consciousness reflected in ignorance as delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Alternatively, the Lord is the consciousness reflected in ignorance.

According to the authors of the *Saṅkṣepaśārīraka*, the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*), whereas the pure consciousness is the original image (*bimba-caitanya*) conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
In these two views, the plurality of souls arises from the diversity of the intellects.
And because the reflection is ultimately real, there is only *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication) in words such as "That" (*tat*) and "Thou" (*tvam*).
This very [view] they call the *pratibimbavāda* (theory of reflection).
Consciousness that has become the object of ignorance is the Lord (*īśvara*).
And Vācaspatimiśra maintains that the individual soul (jīva) is the substratum of ignorance;
and according to this view, because ignorance is manifold, the souls are manifold, and for each soul there is a distinct phenomenal world (prapañca).
Because the individual soul (jīva) alone, being conditioned by its own ignorance, is the material cause (upādāna) of the world;
and because recognition (pratyabhijñā) occurs due to extreme similarity;

and because God (īśvara) is metaphorically designated as the cause by virtue of being the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) for the ignorance of the individual soul along with its phenomenal world (saprapañca).
And this very [view] is the theory of limitation (avacchedavāda):
either that the Lord (īśvara) is the mirror-consciousness (bimba-caitanya) conditioned by ignorance (ajñāna), while the individual soul (jīva) is the consciousness reflected in ignorance; or...
Alternatively, pure consciousness unconditioned by ignorance is the Lord (Īśvara), while consciousness conditioned by ignorance is the individual soul (jīva);
this is the primary Vedānta doctrine known as Ekajīvavāda (the theory of the single soul).
And this very doctrine is called the theory of "creation-as-perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda).

According to this view, it is the individual soul (jīva) alone who, through the power of its own ignorance, is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the world; furthermore, everything that is perceived is merely illusory.
And from the distinction of bodies arises the delusion of a distinction among individual souls (*jīva*).

Liberation occurs when, for one and the same person, there is the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) through the strengthening of hearing, reflection, and so forth, augmented by a teacher and scriptures imagined by oneself.
Furthermore, the scriptural accounts of the liberation of Śuka and others are merely *arthavāda* (laudatory or explanatory statements).

Furthermore, within the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), the term *tat*—like terms such as *ananta* (infinite) and *satya* (truth)—conveys consciousness unconditioned by ignorance through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*); these and other internal distinctions should be inferred by oneself.
Now, one might object: "Since conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are impossible regarding a real entity (*vastu*), how can there be the validity of mutually contradictory doctrines?
Therefore, what here is to be rejected and what is to be accepted? If this is asked:

Who says that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), given that conceptual constructions such as "Is it a post, a person, or a *rākṣasa*? are observed even regarding real entities?
That construction is unreal; it arises solely from the human intellect.
If you argue that this is the scriptural arrangement regarding the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara),
then you are surely very clever!
For it is the non-dual reality of the Self (advitīyātmatattva) that is the primary subject matter of the scripture, because it is fruitful and because it is unknown.

However, conceptual constructions such as the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), although originating solely from human intellect, are restated in the scripture because they are useful for the knowledge of reality;

this is according to the maxim that "that which is fruitless in proximity to that which is fruitful is an auxiliary to it," since there is the possibility of the scripture restating even what is established through error.
By this, the sublation of non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*) by dualistic knowledge (*dvaitajñāna*) is refuted;
for there is a rule that the knowledge of duality, such as that of a pot and so forth, must have the same locus and object [as its sublated counterpart],
and because ignorance is not admitted with respect to insentient objects due to the absence of both a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and a purpose (*prayojana*).
For even in that case, the conventional usage of "ignorance" is established precisely because of ignorance regarding the consciousness delimited by that [object],
since validity consists in making known what was previously unknown;
otherwise, it would follow that even memory would possess such validity.
In all cases of such contradictions throughout the Vedāntas, this alone is the resolution.
Thus say the venerable authors of the Vārttika (BAUBhV I.4.402):
"By whatever means people may attain comprehension of the inner self..."
That very process is to be known as the correct one, and that indeed is the established rule. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, we have proclaimed hundreds of times that anything contrary to the meaning intended by the Śruti must indeed be rejected;
therefore, this [objection] amounts to nothing.

Now, if it is asked: "Granted that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as the specific determination of each object of cognition such as the means and objects of knowledge, exists due to the power of ignorance (avidyā); how is this so?"—it is replied:

Although ignorance (*avidyā*) is limited by virtue of its being perceptible and subject to destruction, it is nonetheless indefinable and incapable of withstanding inquiry; possessing two powers—obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*)—it veils the all-pervading conscious Self (*cidātman*), just as a finger placed before the eye veils the solar disc.
For if it were to veil the eye alone, it would follow that the finger itself could not be perceived.
Furthermore, since distraction is impossible without a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
that [unmanifested nature], being impelled by the karma of the living being (*jīva*) and its preceding latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), transforms itself into the form of the entire world.

And because it has attained identity with consciousness (*citta*) through the medium of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) inherent within it, all its effects as well are indeed permeated by consciousness through that very medium of reflection.

And thus, because consciousness—like a lamp—illuminates everything with which it is connected, the consciousness that is the material cause of the world illuminates everything at all times without depending on any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); it is therefore omniscient. Consequently, the distinction between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge (*meya*) does not exist there. However, in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), because it is delimited by being conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi-avacchinnatva*), it is limited; and thus, through that [intellect] which is capable of manifesting consciousness— [The sentence continues: ...[the soul perceives]. Therefore, the distinction between the knower and the known exists for the *jīva*, but not for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, the entire universe is established as having consciousness as its essence. This is the conclusion. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Theory of the World's Being an Illusion," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, composed by the venerable Citsukha. Since the individual soul (*jīva*) experiences only that which is connected to whichever internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) it is associated with at any given time, there is no possibility of confusion between different experiences.
The process here is as follows: situated within the body, [the *jīva*] pervades the entire body by virtue of its predominance of the quality of *sattva*.

The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is a transformation of ignorance (avidyā) composed of the subtle five elements, is extremely transparent like a mirror. Having emerged through the gates of the eyes and other senses, it pervades suitable objects such as jars and assumes their respective forms, just like molten copper. Furthermore, its contraction and expansion occur instantaneously, like sunlight.

And that [internal organ], undergoing transformation because it possesses parts, pervades the interior of the body as well as objects such as jars; it remains even between the body and the jar, like the eye, though it is not divided.

Therein, the portion of the internal organ delimited by the body is called the "agent" (kartṛ), known as the ego (ahaṅkāra). The portion extending like a staff between the body and the object, known as "functional cognition" (vṛttijñāna), is called the "action" (kriyā).
The portion of the internal organ that pervades the object is called the "fitness for manifestation" (*abhivyakti-yogyatva*), which brings about the status of the object as the content of knowledge.
Because this threefold internal organ is extremely transparent, consciousness is manifested therein.
Although that manifested consciousness is one, it receives a threefold designation due to the distinctions among the portions of the internal organ that manifest it.

The aspect of consciousness delimited by the agent-part is the knower (*pramātṛ*); the aspect of consciousness delimited by the action-part is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and the aspect of consciousness delimited by the part consisting in the fitness for manifestation residing in the object is the resulting cognition (*pramiti*).
The object of knowledge (*prameya*), however, is simply the Brahman-consciousness residing within the objective sphere when it is unknown;
that very same consciousness, when known, is the fruit (*phala*).
And in this regard, according to the view in which the individual soul (*jīva*) is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [the following applies].

In the view where the individual soul (*jīva*) is all-pervading, unattached, and a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*), in both cases the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) serves the purpose of coloring the consciousness of the knower and the purpose of breaking the veil over the object-consciousness. In the view, however, where the all-pervading *jīva* is delimited by ignorance and remains veiled, since the *jīva* itself is the material cause of the world and is thus connected to everything, the mental modification serves solely the purpose of breaking that veil.
Such is the distinction.

Now, an objection is raised: if the position is that a mental modification (*vṛtti*) exists for the purpose of coloring consciousness (*cid-uparāga*), then merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth—which are inherently connected to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—as well as Brahman, would always be manifest even without a modification.
This is not so, because consciousness lacks the form (*ākāra*) of those respective objects.
And that absence [of manifestation] occurs either because of obscuration, even in the case of the pure consciousness of Brahman;
or because of lack of clarity, even in the case of unobscured things such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
or, in the case of dharma, adharma, and so forth, because of both lack of clarity and obscuration.
Therefore, even when [the self] is clear, it assumes the form of that [object] through the operation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

however, in the case of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which are clear and unobscured, [this occurs] spontaneously. Thus, there is no undesirable consequence of these appearing merely through their connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Now, one might ask: how can there be an obscuration of Brahman?
Because it is omniscient by virtue of its own faultless self-luminosity.

True; although it is omniscient insofar as it illuminates everything connected to itself, it is nevertheless designated as "veiled" because it is the object of the ignorance of the individual soul (*jīva*) delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Therefore, according to the view that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) serves both to bring about the reflection of consciousness (*ciduparāga*) and to effect the destruction of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*).
But on the view that the individual soul (jīva) is the material cause [of the world], [the scripture] serves solely for the purpose of destroying the veil.
Now, an objection is raised: if the veil were destroyed by a single cognition of a jar or the like, it would follow that liberation occurs immediately, because ignorance (ajñāna) is one.

Even in the view that there are multiple ignorances (*nānājñāna*), [the objection does not hold] because a single individual soul (*jīva*) possesses only a single limiting adjunct of ignorance (*ekājñānopādhi*).
This is not so, because it is accepted that the veil of the modification (*vṛtti-āvaraṇa*) is overcome by the [cognition], just as a gem is affected by a catalyst (*uttejaka*).

Thus, ignorance—conjoined with the absence of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is called a "veiling" (*āvaraṇa*) because it has the capacity to produce the cognition "it does not exist" and "it does not appear," even when the object is present and shining.

But once the transformation (*vṛtti*) has arisen, because there is no longer any delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), even though ignorance (*avidyā*) still exists, it is as if non-existent; thus, being overcome by that [transformation], it is said to be incapable of its own effects.
[Objection: But if this were so, since ignorance would not be removed even by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), the consequence would follow that liberation (*mokṣa*) is impossible.
[Reply: No, for it is accepted that ignorance is removed through the knowledge of the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

Because it sublates ignorance precisely by being a valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding its own object, the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) alone possesses validity due to having an unsublated object;

whereas perception and the other means of knowledge, although they are errors because their objects are sublated, are regarded as valid due to their functional efficacy in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
The absence of [ignorance] elsewhere than through the cessation of ignorance by means of knowledge is irrelevant,
because it is established by one's own experience and because the principle of "otherwise being impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*) is more powerful than anything else.
As it has been said [in the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya* 1]:
"If there is 'inexplicability otherwise' (*anyathānupapatti*) which establishes a real entity, that very principle, being superior in all power, grinds away the disagreement regarding non-existence."
Alternatively, the various states of ignorance (*avasthājñāna*) are themselves the veils over objects such as jars;

since it is accepted that there are as many ignorances as there are cognitions—ignorance standing in the place of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge—the destruction of a single ignorance occurs through a single cognition.
Thus, even when the veil is destroyed by the cognition of a jar or the like, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Now, does the veil cease through inference and other means, or not?

In the first case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even an erroneous cognition that is directly perceptual—such as the yellowness of a conch shell—would cease through inference of its whiteness and so forth;
for since the error has ignorance regarding the substrate as its material cause, it must cease when that [ignorance] ceases.

Furthermore, if ignorance were removed from Brahman by rational knowledge alone, there would be no need for hearing, reflection, and so forth, for the sake of direct realization. In the second case, however, the practical usage of fire and such things would not be possible,
because the obstacle [of ignorance] would still be present.
It is said: obscuration is of two kinds;

one is that which brings about non-existence (asattva) and resides in the witness (sākṣin) as delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); the other is that which brings about non-manifestation (abhāna) and resides in the Brahman-consciousness as delimited by the object (viṣaya).

Because there is an experience of the limitation by both [negations] in the cognition "I do not know the jar," therein the first [negation] is removed by mere valid cognition (pramā) common to both the indirect (parokṣa) and the direct (aparokṣa),
since the cognition "it does not exist" does not arise even when fire and such have been inferred.
The second [type of ignorance], however, is removed by direct realization alone;
for there is a rule that knowledge which is established upon a certain object and possesses a certain form destroys the ignorance established upon that same object and possessing that same form,
because [the two] are respectively non-manifest and manifest.
As it has been said (Pañca 7.45):
"Through indirect knowledge, the state of being a cause for the veil of non-existence is destroyed;
through direct cognition, the state of being a cause for the veil of non-appearance is destroyed."
Therefore, because inference and the like destroy the veil over non-existence, they function with respect to that [object];
and by the cessation of the veil over non-appearance, there occurs the cessation of the error consisting in a qualified direct perception.

Consequently, even for the Self which is devoid of attributes, the superimposition of its attributes—such as agency and enjoyership—is possible through the superimposition of identity with ignorance and the internal organ.

Now, in your view, since the theory of indeterminable manifestation (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*) is accepted, it must be stated that those attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) such as agency (*kartṛtva*) which are superimposed upon the Self arise there as indeterminable.
And in that case, there would be a twofold appearance of agency, enjoyership, and so forth, by way of the distinction between the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and the apparent (*prātītika*).
It would not [be so], because there is no discrimination due to the conceit of identity (*tādātmyābhimāna*);
or rather, because of the absence of duality, since it is precisely the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), as qualified by all its attributes, that is superimposed upon the Self.

Therefore, since the distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth is established through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the one and only Self, there is neither a lapse into the Buddhist position nor any contradiction.
Other systematic arrangements will be demonstrated more clearly below.

Therefore, since the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is non-deviant during deep sleep, whereas the body, senses, and so forth are deviant and are objects of perception, the notion of the Self attributed to those various disputants regarding them is an illusion; such is the doctrine of the Upaniṣads.
Thus, it is established that this alone is the means of valid cognition. // 1 //

It might be argued as follows: if the self were devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) and the conventional usage of the knower and so forth were rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*), then scriptures such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" would result in being invalid (*aprāmāṇya*);
for activity would be impossible for a self that is neither an agent nor an enjoyer. And if the Veda were invalid, how could even Brahman be established?
Because that [Brahman] is accessible through that alone,
according to the principle that "the scripture is its source" (*śāstrayonitva*);
and thus, having raised the objection that for the sake of the authority of the Veda, the reality of the conventional usage of the knower and so forth must be admitted—

Does invalidity arise prior to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), or subsequent to it? Regarding the first case, since the established state of the cessation of ignorance has been demonstrated, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ignorance as their object; therefore, in that state, because there is no sublation (*bādhā*), their validity remains unimpeded. As for the second case, it is simply what we accept. Thus he says:
There are no castes, nor the duties of the stages of life and conduct; nor do I possess dhāraṇā, meditation, yoga, and the like.
Because of the abandonment of the superimposition of "I" and "mine" upon that which is not the Self, I alone remain—that one, auspicious, and absolute.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
the *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra;
and the *āśramas* are the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*).
*Ācāras* are practices such as ritual purity and bathing;
*dharmas* are duties such as celibacy and service to the teacher.

Here, by means of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound containing two internal *dvandva*s, both the practices and duties of the social classes (*varṇas*) and the practices and duties of the stages of life (*āśramas*) are obtained.

Dhāraṇā is the steadiness of the mind through the abandonment of external objects upon the Brahman. Dhyāna is the contemplation of the Supreme Self. Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), hearing, reflection, and so forth are included.

He states the reason why all these cease to exist after the arising of knowledge: "because of the abandonment of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of 'I' and 'mine,' which have the non-self (*anātman*) as their substrate.
Here, the non-self (*anātman*) is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the opposite of the Self (*ātman*).

The meaning is that because the superimposition (adhyāsa) of "I" and "mine" and so forth— which has that [ignorance] as its locus and that [ignorance] as its material cause— is abandoned along with its root by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), the worldly transaction (vyavahāra) involving caste, stage of life, and so on, which is prompted by that [superimposition], no longer exists. To confirm the falsity of the transaction of caste, stage of life, and so on— since it is rooted solely in false knowledge— he states the negative concomitance (vyatireka) in deep sleep, which is the absence of that [superimposition].
Neither mother nor father, nor gods, nor worlds, nor deities, nor sacrifices, nor sacred fords speak;
because in deep sleep one's nature is utterly void and free from distinctions, that alone remains—I am Śiva, the absolute. // 3 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
"Mother" refers to the female progenitor;
"father" refers to the male progenitor.
The gods, such as Indra and others, are those to be propitiated;
the worlds are the fruits of their propitiation, such as heaven and so forth;
and the gods are the authoritative statements that establish Brahman and set forth the means for achieving what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful in a manner transcending the ordinary world.
Sacrifices (*yajña*) refer to rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* which serve as means for attaining heaven and other goals;
sacred sites (*tīrtha*) refer to regions such as Kurukṣetra which serve as means for performing sacrifices.
In this manner, those things that serve as means for committing sinful acts should also be understood by implication.

The meaning is that because all [these distinctions] are rendered mute by the conceit of the body (*dehābhimāna*), they do not exist when that [conceit] is absent, due to the lack of any inherent connection.

Thus, with reference to deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the Śruti says: "In this state, the father is no longer a father, the mother is no longer a mother, the gods are no longer gods, and the Vedas are no longer Vedas;
the thief becomes a non-thief, the slayer of an embryo becomes a non-slayer, the outcaste (*caṇḍāla*) becomes a non-outcaste, the *paulkasa* becomes a non-*paulkasa*, and the ascetic..."
"Then the ascetic becomes a non-ascetic, untouched by merit and untouched by evil; for he has then crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22).
Passages such as these restate that, in the absence of conceit, there is the cessation of all objects of experience.
[Objection: But surely, in the absence of all conventional discourse, there would be only emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
[Reply: No; thus he says: "because its nature as an extreme emptiness has been discarded.
That from which the nature of extreme emptiness has been discarded is "that which is so" (*tathā*).
This is an indication where the abstract state is primary,
because that [state] is the means for deep sleep and because a subsequent rising would otherwise be impossible:
"Verily, this Self is indestructible, O Maitreyī, its nature is such that it does not perish" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14).
“Yet there is for him association with the measure,” “Or rather, when he does not see this, he is indeed seeing though he does not see” (BAU 4.3.23),
“For there is no loss of the seer’s sight.”

The meaning is that, according to scriptural passages such as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad— “Because of its indestructibility, there is no second thing, other than and distinct from it, which it might see”— the consciousness of the Self does not become void even in deep sleep.
Although this has already been refuted, it is refuted once again according to the maxim of "driving in a post" (sthūṇānikhanana-nyāya).
Or rather, because [the individual self] has that as its essence—namely, Brahman, which is beyond hunger and so forth, non-dual, and the supreme void;
and thus the Śruti says: "When, my dear, a person is said to sleep, then he has become united with Being (sat)."

"Just as one embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without nor within, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), knows nothing without nor within" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.9.1).

Therefore, it is established that because of his identity with Brahman—which is the cause of the universe and consists of omniscience, omnipotence, and perfect bliss-consciousness—the individual soul (jīva) is indeed non-transmigratory. // 3 //
The second section:
Determination of the Meaning of That Word (*tatpadārtha-nirṇaya*).
Thus, first of all, by means of three verses, the meaning of the word "Thou" (*tvampadārtha*) has been determined after refuting the divergent views of disputants.
Now, the meaning of that term [Brahman] must likewise be determined.
In this regard, the conflicting views of various disputants (vādins) which are to be refuted are presented.
[Objection: Indeed, the identity of Brahman with the individual soul (jīva) is not logically tenable.
For instance, Brahman, the cause of the world denoted by the word "Being," is established by such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
And the Sāṅkhyas maintain that the cause of the world is Pradhāna, which is insentient.
The Pāśupatas maintain that Paśupati alone is the cause of the world; he is conscious yet distinct from the individual soul (jīva), and he alone is the object of worship.
[The Vaiṣṇavas hold that] the Lord Vāsudeva is the sovereign cause of the world.
From that, the individual soul (jīva) named Saṅkarṣaṇa arises;
from that, the mind (manas), Pradyumna; and from that, the ego (ahaṅkāra), Aniruddha.
Therefore, because the individual soul (jīva) is an effect, the followers of the Pañcarātra maintain that there is no absolute non-difference between it and Brahman Vāsudeva.
The Jains and the Tridaṇḍins hold that [the soul] is subject to modification, eternal, omniscient, and both different and non-different [from the Lord].
Others maintain that there is no Brahman endowed with omniscience and other such qualities.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that because the Veda is intent upon ritual action, it lacks any ultimate purport regarding [the existence of] God; rather, like the "speech-cow" (vāgdhenū) and other such metaphors, the object of meditation is either the cause of the world—such as atoms—or the individual soul (jīva), characterized by qualities such as omniscience.
[They argue: "There exists no Lord who possesses eternal knowledge and so forth, nor any omniscient being inferred from the evidence of effects such as the earth."
The logicians (Tārkikas) maintain that it [the Lord] is indeed distinct from the individual soul (jīva).
The Buddhists (Saugatas) hold that he is momentary and omniscient.

The followers of Patañjali (Pātañjalas) maintain that he is untouched by afflictions, karma, its fruition, or latent dispositions; that his nature is eternal knowledge; that he is omniscient by virtue of being reflected through the quality of *sattva*, which is a constituent of *pradhāna*; and that he is entirely distinct from the transmigrating individual souls (*saṃsāri-puruṣa*).
The Upaniṣadic teachers maintain that Brahman is indeed non-dual supreme bliss,

and that it is the actual nature of the individual soul (jīva), which, through Māyā, is characterized by omniscience and so forth, and serves as both the material cause and the efficient cause of the world.

Since the referent of the word "That" (tatpadārtha) is thus rendered doubtful by these conflicting views of various disputants, the Blessed Lord speaks in order to determine it through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) in favor of the Upaniṣadic position:
Neither the Sāṅkhya, nor the Śaiva, nor that Pāñcarātra, nor this [Vedānta], nor the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas and others;
because of its nature as the pure Self through distinguished experience, I am that one who remains—the solitary Śiva. // 4 //
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those not explicitly mentioned are included.
First of all, the insentient world cannot be the material cause [of itself], because [the scripture] says: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.2.3).
Because the scripture records creation preceded by such contemplation,
and because there is the designation of the Self as the individual soul in the passage: "Having entered with this living self, let me evolve names and forms" (ChU VI.3.2).
Furthermore, because of the promise that through the knowledge of one thing everything becomes known— expressed in the passage, "When that is known, all this becomes known" (MU I.1.3)—
and because it is impossible to know the individual souls (*puruṣa*), which do not have the *pradhāna* as their material cause, by means of knowing the *pradhāna*.
And because of the ninefold instruction regarding non-difference from That in the passage, “All this has that as its essence; that is the Truth; that is the Self;
thou art That” (ChU VI.8.7), and [because of the statement], “From this very Self, indeed, ether was produced” (TU II.1).
Thus, because of another Vedic scripture stating that a non-conscious entity cannot be the cause of the world— since a variegated arrangement would be impossible—

and because the *pradhāna*, *mahat*, and so forth lack scriptural authority, the Sāṅkhya doctrine is not tenable. Likewise, the Pāśupata, Pāñcarātrika, and Jaina doctrines are untenable, as they are contradicted by both scripture and reasoning.

Nor is the Mīmāṃsaka position—that the Śruti does not establish Brahman because it is supplementary to an injunction (vidhiśeṣatva)—tenable, because that status as a supplement to an injunction is unproven.
Nor can its being supplementary to an injunction be established by the logic of the section on Arthavādas (Arthavādādhikaraṇa), because of the disparity between the cases;
for [the texts in question] do not, in themselves, convey a purposeful meaning such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" (TS II.1.1.1).
Since the inclusion of these [Arthavādas] under the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) would otherwise be inexplicable, they must be assumed to have a purposeful meaning. Thus,

it has been determined in the *Arthavāda* section that because the injunction— which requires the constituent elements of the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*), namely its object and its procedure— completes that procedural element by means of praising the deities who are its recipients, there is a syntactic unity between the two (the injunction and the Arthavāda) according to the maxim of "the lost horse and the burnt chariot" (*naṣṭāśvadagdharathanyāya*).

Furthermore, since the attainment of supreme bliss and the cessation of all suffering—the very goals of human endeavor—are obtained directly from the knowledge produced by the Vedānta texts, there is no possibility of these texts being subordinate to anything else, as they leave no further desire unfulfilled. On the contrary, it is the injunctions themselves that are subordinate to the Vedānta through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*). Thus, because of their own inherent authority, the existence of Brahman is indeed established; the position of the Mīmāṃsakas is not proven.
Nor is the view of the logicians (*tārkika*) and others tenable regarding the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
“I am Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10);
“This Self is Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19);
“Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
This is sublated by such scriptural passages as:
"Brahman is one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "There is not here any diversity whatsoever" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).

Furthermore, [the views] such as being both different and non-different, and momentariness, are contradicted by scriptural texts (*śruti*) such as, "He is omnipresent and eternal like space. And here,
since the non-existence of all [these] positions has been asserted, the reason (*hetu*) is "because of having the nature of pure selfhood" (*viśuddhātmakatvāt*).
The meaning is: "because its nature is non-conceptual and non-dual consciousness.
The reason for this is stated as "by means of a specific experience" (*viśiṣṭānubhūtyā*).
This means: by that indivisible experience produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which is distinguished—that is, set apart—from conceptual experiences (*savikalpakānubhūti*).
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is all-pervading, non-dual, and consists of the nature of supreme bliss and consciousness. // 4 //

But is it not the case that, because of the scriptural texts regarding the minuteness of Brahman— such as "That which is this subtle essence" (ChU VI.8.15) and "More minute than the minute" (TA X.12.1, KU I.2.20, SvU III.20)— [Brahman must be atomic]?

Raising the objection that Brahman cannot be all-pervasive because it is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*), which is taught in such scriptural passages as “The Person is the size of a thumb” (KU II.4.12) and “Indeed, even the lower [self] is seen to be the size of the tip of an awl” (SvU V.8), [the text continues]: “This immortal Brahman is indeed before; Brahman is behind; Brahman is to the south...”
“And by the north; spread below and above, this entire universe is Brahman alone, the most excellent” (MU II.2.11);
“This very Brahman is without before, without after, without within, without without” (BAU II.5.11).
Reinforcing what was stated previously—that the aforementioned scriptural passages establish Brahman as being indeed devoid of distinctions—he says:

"Neither above nor below, neither within nor without, neither in the middle nor across, nor in the eastern or western direction; because it pervades space, it is of an indivisible and uniform nature. That alone remains—Śiva, the absolute, I am He. (5)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

because it is all-pervading like space (*viyat*), due to its pervasiveness being like that of space, according to the Vedic scripture, "And like space, it is omnipresent and eternal" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.9.1); or alternatively, because space itself is all-pervading, [it is said], "[He is] greater than space" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* X.6.3.2).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Greater than the great" (KU II.20).
Furthermore, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is also "great" insofar as its consciousness is perceived as pervading the entire body, [it is not the Supreme Self].
This is because the description of [the soul] as being "only the size of the tip of a goad" occurs through the superimposition of the attributes of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

for the scripture states, "By the quality of the intellect and by its own quality, it is seen to be even smaller than the tip of a goad" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.8), and the designation of Brahman as "atomic" is intended to express its subtlety.
The remainder has its meaning not concealed. // 5 //

Now, one might object: since Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, and because there is non-difference between the material cause and its effect (*upādeya*), Brahman is non-different from the diverse world;

thus, because Brahman possesses the nature of suffering, the individual soul (*jīva*), being non-different from it, could not attain the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that because Brahman consists of self-luminous supreme bliss (*svaprakāśaparamānanda*), it is designated as the "cause" only insofar as it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the illusion of the entire world.
And because there is no relationship with that which is superimposed, not even a trace of evil exists therein; thus he says:
Neither white, nor black, nor red, nor yellow; neither humpbacked, nor stout, nor short, nor long.
Formless, likewise, is that Light because it is devoid of form; I am that alone, the one, Śiva, the absolute. (6)
The small is minute;
the large is great.
By this negation of the fourfold dimensions—namely, minute, great, short, and long—there is a negation of its substantiality (*dravyatva*).
That which is manifested is "form" (rūpa), that is, the object of cognition (prameya).
That which is not an object of cognition is "formless" (arūpa).
By this, there is a negation of all categories such as substance, quality, and action, as they are accepted by their respective proponents.
And thus the Śruti declares: "Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.8.8), and so forth;

and "That which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad I.3.15), and so forth—all such passages establish that the nature of the Supreme Self is devoid of all defects.
He states the reason for determining even the meaning of the Śruti through logic: "because it has the nature of light.
This is because, being of the nature of self-luminous knowledge, it is not an object of cognition;
for if it were an object of cognition, it would follow that it is insentient, like a jar or other such objects.
The meaning is that this is also because of such scriptural passages as, "This is immeasurable and eternal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.4.20). // 6 //
The third section:
Determining the Meaning of the Statement "That Thou Art" (Tattvamasi).
Now, to whom is the state of being Brahman taught?
Whether [the teacher] be a Brahmin or a non-Brahmin:
not the latter, because he is insentient and lacks existence;
nor the former, because instruction would be purposeless.
Because the state of being Brahman is established by its own nature.
If it is argued that although the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman by its own nature, the obstruction of ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed by knowledge, we say no;
for if the cessation of ignorance were distinct from the Self, dualism would result, leading to the undesirable consequence that Brahman remains unestablished.
Thus it is said in the Vārttika (BAUBhV II.4.14): "That which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else is called Brahman;
the true meaning of Brahman cannot be found here as long as there exists a second entity."
And it has been stated that if there were no distinction [between the two], instruction would be purposeless.
In this regard, do you intend that there is an absence of result from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), or even from the perspective of conventional cognition (pratīti)?
Regarding the first case, he refutes it by accepting it as a desired consequence (iṣṭāpatti):
There is no teacher, no scripture, no disciple, no training, neither you, nor I, nor this conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The realization of one's own true nature, which cannot endure conceptual construction—that alone remains: I am the solitary, auspicious Śiva. (7)
The teacher is the one who provides instruction;
the teaching is the act of providing instruction;
and the disciple is the object of the instruction.
Training is the practice of instruction;
you are the listener,
and I am the speaker.

The meaning is that this manifold world, consisting of the body, sense organs, and so forth— an entity brought into proximity by all means of valid cognition— is, in the ultimate sense, a non-entity and does not exist.
He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "svarūpa" (its own nature).

This is the meaning: although it is impossible to determine any specific result by conceptualizing whether the cessation of ignorance is the Self or the non-Self, nevertheless, the realization of one's own true nature (*svarūpāvabodha*) is the fruit of knowledge (*vijñāna*).
Nor should it be questioned how this is so, because [this realization], having sublated all duality, cannot tolerate conceptualization.
For indeed, there is nothing that is untenable when it is directly perceived;
and thus says the Śruti (Gauḍapāda-Kārikā II.32):
"There is neither cessation nor origination, neither one bound nor one who strives for liberation."
Neither one desiring liberation nor one who is liberated—this is the ultimate truth.”
“In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman.
It knew only itself as ‘I am Brahman,’ and therefore it became all this. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad I.4.7)
