Thus, the aforementioned passage also demonstrates that the individual soul (jīva), which even previously existed as having the very nature of Brahman, attains the state of Brahman through knowledge, and it negates all duality. // 7 //
If it is objected: "But if the Self is of the nature of self-luminosity and remains always the same, how can there be the distinction between the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth?
Nor should it be said that this distinction is due to mere illusion, for if that were so, everything would necessarily be a dream"—we reply: No.

From the perspective of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), although all three are equally dream-like, a distinction is possible because an ignorance-based difference manifests; yet, since they possess specific qualities by virtue of being distinct from the non-existent, a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is established. However, from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no such arrangement at all, as he says:
"Neither waking nor dream nor deep sleep belongs to me; neither the *viśva*, nor the *taijasa*, nor the *prājña* exists."
Because the triad consists of ignorance, that which remains as the one Fourth is Śiva alone; I am He.
In this context, the sequence is indicated according to the order of dissolution (*layakrama*).
For it is thus: in our system, the categories of existence (*padārtha*) are twofold—the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*).
Because the categories of objects postulated by other proponents are included within these very ones:
therein, the category of the Seer (dṛk-padārtha) is the ultimate Self, which is one and always of a single nature, yet appears threefold through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—
namely, the Lord (īśvara), the individual soul (jīva), and the witness (sākṣin).
In this context, Īśvara is that which has ignorance (ajñāna) as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) when that ignorance functions as the cause;
the jīva is that which is conditioned by ignorance delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and its impressions (saṃskāra).
This has been explained in detail below.

In the view that the Lord is a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is the consciousness of the original (*bimba*) that is called the Witness (*sākṣin*); and in the view that the Lord is the original, it is the consciousness that pervades both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord— just as the face itself pervades both the original face and its reflection— which, as the synthesizer of all, is called the Witness.
According to the view of the author of the Vārttika, however, the witness is indeed only Īśvara; thus, the twofold division is seen as that between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
Among these, Īśvara is also threefold:

by virtue of the distinction among the three qualities (guṇas) of his own limiting adjunct (upādhi), which is ignorance (avidyā), Viṣṇu—conditioned by rajas—is the cause [of preservation]; Brahmā is the creator.

Hiraṇyagarbha, however, is not Brahmā because he lacks the status of being the cause of the great elements (*mahābhūta*); nevertheless, because he is the creator of the gross elements, he is sometimes called Brahmā.
Rudra, presided over by *tamas* which has become the instrumental cause, is the destroyer.
And thus, for this very [one], there are male forms such as the four-armed, the four-faced, and the five-faced, as well as female forms such as Śrī, Bhāratī, and Bhvānī.

Furthermore, it should be understood that other infinite incarnations, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth, manifest through mere play for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees; for the scripture states: "The conceptualization of forms for Brahman—who is composed of consciousness, non-dual, partless, and bodiless—is for the sake of the needs of those who worship."
The individual soul (jīva) is also threefold,
distinguished as Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña according to the internal subdivisions of its own limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Among these, the Viśva is that which is delimited by ignorance (avidyā), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and the gross body (sthūla-śarīra), and identifies with the waking state.

That very [Self], when devoid of identification with the gross body and conditioned by the two adjuncts (the subtle body and the internal organ), is the Taijasa, characterized by the identification with the dream state.

When devoid of the two adjuncts—the body and the internal organ—and conditioned solely by ignorance delimited by the impressions of the internal organ, it is the Prājña, characterized by the identification with deep sleep.

Although there is no independent distinction among these due to the absence of independent adjuncts, a subordinate distinction is spoken of despite their essential unity, owing to the difference between the subordinate adjuncts.
The witness, however, which synthesizes all, which pervades all, and is called the fourth (*turya*), is of only one kind.
Even there, no differentiation occurs even through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because that limiting adjunct is of a single nature.
The phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of ignorance, its pervasions, and its effects, is the category of the object of perception (*dṛśya*).

And although that [unmanifest] is not ultimately real, its investigation is not useless— unlike dream-objects— because its conventional existence is admitted and because it is useful for practices such as meditation (*upāsanā*).
That too is threefold, based on the distinction between the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the formless (*amūrta*), and the formed (*mūrta*).

In this context, *avidyā* accompanied by its reflection (*sābhāsāvidyā*)—which exists in the form of the causal power (*bījaśakti*) for the manifold of manifest and unmanifest phenomena—is called "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*). Although it is not produced by that [pure Consciousness], it ceases upon the cessation of that [Consciousness] and is therefore pervaded by it; thus, because it is beginningless along with consciousness, its relation to it, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), it is termed "unmanifest. And although it is itself insentient (*jaḍa*), being impelled by the karma of the individual soul and ignited by the non-insentient reflection of consciousness through the impressions of successive prior states, it [produces] the elements known as ether, air, fire, water, and earth, which consist of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

It produces the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtāni*). In this regard, because ignorance—which has assumed the state of each preceding element—is the cause for each subsequent one, the qualities of each preceding element permeate the subsequent elements. Thus, from ignorance itself, darkness (*andhakāra*) also arises; it is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), consisting of non-light (*ālokātmā*), opposed to visual cognition, and destroyed by light. Like a great flash of lightning and so forth, it suddenly manifests and disappears.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Furthermore, because [the self] lacks the nature of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the body—which is the cause of transmigratory existence—it is taught in the Vedic scriptures within the process of creation; thus, there is no contradiction.
As for space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*), they are not mentioned because they lack scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*).

Since it is possible to establish that space alone generates the conventional usage of "directions," and because of the Vedic scripture stating, "The ear is the direction" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.2.13),
time is indeed nescience (avidyā) itself, as it alone is the substratum of all things.

And this indeterminate category is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Īśvara. These five great elements, though subtle and unevolved (apañcīkṛta), are called "formless" because of their identity with the cause; they consist of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Due to the predominance of the sattva portion, that part characterized primarily by the powers of knowledge and action is prāṇa.
And that [vital breath] is fivefold:
prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
Thus, from each of the individual elements, two sense organs arise respectively due to the differentiation of the powers of knowledge and action.
From space come the ear and speech;
from wind, the skin and the hands; from fire, the eye and the feet.
From water come the tongue and the anus; from earth come the nose and the generative organ.
In this regard, it is said: "Speech consists of fire" (ChU VI.5.4).
According to this Vedic scripture, some maintain that speech is composed of fire (taijasa) while the feet are composed of ether (nābhasa);
however, because speech is a sense organ that manifests sound, it possesses the nature of ether (nābhasatva), just like the ear.
Furthermore, since we observe the restoration of health to the eye through medical treatment of the feet, we consider it logical that the feet, like the eye, possess a fiery nature (*taijasatva*).

As for the scriptural statement regarding its being composed of light (*tejomaya*), it should be explained as referring to the mind’s dependence on that [light], just as the scriptural statement regarding the mind being "composed of food" (*annamaya*)—despite the mind being an effect of the five elements—is explained by its dependence on food.

Moreover, the fact that the mind consists of the five elements is a separate matter altogether, established by the certainty that it possesses those [elements] because it perceives the qualities of the five elements.
The presiding deities of these [senses] are also primarily characterized by the powers of knowledge and action: Dig and Agni,
Vāta and Indra.
Āditya and Viṣṇu, Varuṇa and Mitra, the Aśvins and Prajāpati.

In that context, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the collective totality of the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*), and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the collective totality of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
The five sense organs of cognition— known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell— are the perceivers of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, respectively.
The skin and the eyes grasp not only their own respective objects of perception but also the substance that serves as the locus for those qualities.
The ear, like the eye, reaches out to grasp sound, because of the cognition "the sound is at a distance.
Furthermore, there are five organs of action known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, which respectively produce utterance, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure.

All this taken together constitutes the seventeenfold *liṅga*, which is called *hiraṇyagarbha* when knowledge-power (*jñāna-śakti*) predominates, and *sūtra* when action-power (*kriyā-śakti*) predominates. This formless entity, being an effect, serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) both in its collective and distributive aspects. And those elements, being of such a nature, are unable to produce experience without a body as the locus of experience and objects as the things experienced; for they are impelled by the karma of the soul toward grossification.
They become fivefold (pañcīkṛta).
In that process, each of the five elements is divided into two parts;
there, each single part is further divided into four.

And that [ether] enters into half-portions of each of the other four elements, excluding its own nature; thus, even though there is a combination through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*)—consisting of its own half-portion and one-eighth portion of each of the others—it is designated by terms such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth because of its predominance.
In this regard, [the scripture says]: "I shall make each one threefold, threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.3.3).

Thus, because of the sacred scripture and because of the Sūtra, “Because of the instruction regarding [the elements] making [each] tripartite” (BS II.4.20), some believe that the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) itself is what is perceived as the combination of the three; however, they are refuted by the very same principle applied in the section concerning ether (*viyadadhikaraṇa*).
For instance, in the Taittirīyaka: “From this very Self, indeed, ether was produced... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Although the Chāndogya Upaniṣad mentions the creation of only the three— fire, water, and food— in passages such as "From space, air" (TU II.1.1),

there is nevertheless an inclusion of the other two [ether and air] because the categories of ether and air possess greater force than the category of fire with respect to its status as the first element.
Furthermore, because the *Chāndogya* asserts that through the knowledge of one thing all things are known,
it must necessarily be stated that even insentient entities such as ether (*ākāśa*) and air (*vāyu*) are effects of Brahman.
In that context, although there is a combination of only five elements, the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is logically established by means of a partial reference (*avayutyānuvāda*).

However, if one were to conceive that [the elements] are indeed *trivṛt* (tripartite) only, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, the sūtra, “Because of the teaching regarding that which makes [them] tripartite” (BS II.4.20), being merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), is not capable of subverting the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) established by reasoning.

Furthermore, the perception of "blackness" (melana) in the body and so forth is entirely indistinguishable for all five [elements], and there is the statement of the Commentator: "the five great elements have been quintuplicated" (pañcīkṛta).
Therefore, this reflection on the non-self is useless; such is the direction of the argument.

And those five great elements, having been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*) and designated as "formed" (*mūrta*), combine to produce a single effect: the locus of the sense organs and the abode of experience.
That alone is called the body (*śarīra*).
Among these, that in which *sattva* predominates is the divine body.

The human body has *rajas* as its predominant quality, while the bodies of animals and so forth, down to stationary beings, have *tamas* as their predominant quality. Furthermore, although that body is composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), there is no contradiction in the elements being present in varying proportions— some deficient and some excessive— just as in the case of a variegated painting.

In this way, the objects as well— consisting of each of the five elements in their quintuplicated form (*pañcīkṛta*), known as the fourteen worlds, arranged in upper, middle, and lower divisions, and predominated by the portions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— as well as jars and so forth,
all this is called the "Cosmic Egg" (*brahmāṇḍa*), the "Virāj," and the "Mūrtam.
This is the sequence of creation according to the Upaniṣads.
The reverse of that is the process of dissolution (*layakrama*).

The formal Virāj, which consists of the five gross elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) and their products formed through quintuplication (*pañcīkṛta*), dissolves into its own cause— the formless Hiraṇyagarbha, which consists of the five gross elements prior to quintuplication (*apañcīkṛta*)— through the dissolution of each individual gross element, beginning with earth.
That indeed is the daily dissolution (*dainandinapralaya*).
And the formless [state] resides in the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Supreme Lord.
However, because the unmanifest is beginningless and lacks a cause, there is no dissolution of it.
Dissolution (*laya*) is defined as the subsistence of an entity in its own cause in a subtle form;
this is what constitutes elemental dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*).
Absolute dissolution (*atyantika-pralaya*), however, is the ultimate cessation [of all existence] resulting from the knowledge of Brahman.
And that occurs precisely through the sequence of causes, because the cessation of the effect follows only from the cessation of the cause.

Furthermore, all processes such as creation and dissolution, although not ultimately real—being like the creation and dissolution within a dream—are nonetheless capable of functioning in conventional practice due to the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, even though they are illusory (*māyika*), there is no consequence of their being utterly non-existent.
How this is so is clearly stated in the original source (*ākara*).
This being the case, the classification of the states such as waking and so forth is now described:
waking is the apprehension of objects occurring during the functioning of the sense faculties.

And therein, the embodied object of enjoyment called Virāj—which is termed *vyāvahārika* because it is dealt with by the six means of knowledge such as direct perception—is experienced by the individual soul (*jīva*) known as Viśva.

It is called Viśva because it enters (*praveśa*) or pervades (*vyāpana*) the body, senses, and so forth, according to the traditional grammatical roots: *viśa* in the sense of "entering" and *viṣl* in the sense of "pervading."
In this context, although the unmanifest (*amūrta*) and undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) Viśva is experienced through inference and other means,

nevertheless, because of the rule that everything empirical is known only by the Viśva, and because of his identification with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*), he does not pervade the other states. Furthermore,

although the objects of cognitions such as "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" are non-empirical due to their lack of validity, the state of waking is still possible [for the Viśva] because it occurs at the time of the operation of the sense organs.
The process of the arising of knowledge and so forth has already been explained above.

Thus, when the karma that produces waking experience is exhausted and the karma that produces dream experience arises, the identification with the gross body is removed by an indeterminate (nirākhyā) tamasic mental modification; consequently, because the deities [presiding over] all the sense organs no longer bestow their grace, they become inactive.
When all [the faculties] have dissolved, even the *viśva* is said to be dissolved;
that is the state of dream (*svapnāvasthā*).
In that state, dream is the perception of objects occurring at a time when there is an absence of sensory activity, caused by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Regarding this, some maintain that it is the mind alone that transforms (*vivartate*) into the forms of objects such as elephants and horses, and is perceived through a function of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*). Others hold that ignorance itself transforms into the forms of dream-objects—like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—and is perceived through a function of ignorance.
Which position is superior? The latter.

Because ignorance alone is postulated as the material cause (*upādāna*) for both the superimposition of objects and the superimposition of cognitions everywhere, and because it is designated in some instances as a modification of the mind (*manas-pariṇāma*) due to being caused by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in the mind;

[one might object]: "In that case, if a modification of the mind into the form of the object is not admitted, the self's status as a seer would be possible, and thus its self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) would remain unestablished. [We reply]:

No, because in the absence of a mental mode (*vṛtti*) produced by the external senses, the mind is then not a grasper; for it is a fixed rule that the mind is a grasper only through the cooperation of those [senses].

Since it is a rule that only consciousness (caitanya) as delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) together with its mental modifications (vṛtti) possesses the status of a knower (pramātṛ), there is an absence of a knower even when the internal organ exists [during sleep].

Regarding the locus of the superimposition of dreams, some say it is the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya) delimited by the mind (manas), while others say it is the Brahman-consciousness delimited by root-ignorance (mūlājñāna).
What is the better [view]? Both are [valid] according to different opinions.

For instance: since it is accepted that the cessation of the delusion of a dream occurs through waking awareness, and since the cessation of a delusion results precisely from the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and since Brahman-consciousness is the substrate, there would be no cessation of the dream through waking awareness because, during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), that [Brahman-consciousness] is not known; and since all duality ceases through [the knowledge of] that [Brahman], [the former view holds].

Because of the scriptural statement that "He indeed is the agent" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.3.10), which declares the individual soul (jīva) to be the agent, and because [if Brahman were the substrate] it would follow that the phenomenal world (prapañca) beginning with ether would become common to all [souls], the substrate cannot be Brahman-consciousness as delimited by fundamental ignorance (mūlājñāna).
[Objection: But since the consciousness of the individual soul (jīvacaitanya) is never obscured and is thus always manifest, how can it be the substrate?

[Reply: True; however, even in that case, one must admit a state of ignorance that opposes the manifestation of the empirical aggregate (saṃghāta) conducive to the superimposition (adhyāsa) of dreams.

Furthermore, in the state of dream, one accepts the appearance of another aggregate [of cognition], such as the perception "I am a human" and so forth, just like the perception "I sleep on a bed" which involves a different bed.
Moreover, the absence of the causal complex for such appearance is exactly the same.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the empirical knowledge of aggregates such as "I am a human" is not produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can it have the power to remove ignorance?

If it is argued that, because the alteration of states cannot otherwise be accounted for, one must postulate such a [subsequent] cognition even in deep sleep— a cognition that sublates the dream— and that this is undesirable because it would entail the state of being awake,
then you have spoken well.

Since the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) consists precisely of the knowledge of the dream state accompanied by the dissolution of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is no sublation of that [dream-knowledge] therein. In the waking state, however, because of the experience "the dream appeared as something false," the knowledge "I" is true despite not being produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and since the knowledge of the body and so forth is produced by a means of valid cognition, its opposition to the ignorance of that state is established by experience.

However, the absence of specific knowledge does not cease without a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, since it is established by the very means that apprehend its locus (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) that the Witness (*sākṣin*) lacks the capacity to remove ignorance—precisely because it is the prover of ignorance—there is nothing objectionable here. Moreover, according to the accepted principle that "as many cognitions as there are, so many ignorances," when ignorance is removed by the cognition of the empirical aggregate (*vyāvahārikasaṃghāta*), just as it is by the cognition of mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), [the result follows].

Furthermore, just as in the case of the error regarding silver, there is no impossibility of the superimposition in a dream; thus, on the view that the consciousness of the living individual (*jīvacaitanya*) alone is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no defect whatsoever.

Moreover, when it is accepted that ignorance is removed solely through the knowledge of Brahman, then—just as the error of a snake is suppressed by the error of a staff upon a rope—[the error of the world is likewise suppressed].

Even in the absence of knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no defect whatsoever in the position that the consciousness of Brahman alone is the substrate for the superimposition of dreams, since the dream-delusion can be explained as being eclipsed by the waking-delusion. Furthermore,
the uniqueness of the dream-superimposition for each individual soul follows precisely from the uniqueness of the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) belonging to each.

In this view as well, Brahman-consciousness limited by the mind (*manovacchinna-brahmacaitanya*) alone is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); since it is accepted that the ignorance of the state (*avasthājñāna*) acts as the veil, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
For this very reason, such designations are found here and there in the scriptures.

Now, an objection may be raised: if consciousness limited by the mind were the substratum, then the cognition of an elephant would occur in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), as in "I am an elephant," just as the cognition "this is silver" occurs in coreferentiality with the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*).
If it is argued that— just as in the case of the cognition of silver—

it is not [the case that] "this is an elephant," even under the view that the Brahman-consciousness is the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), the cognition would have to take the form merely of "an elephant" and not "this is an elephant," because in that case too the absence of any external object serving as the locus for the term "this" (idaṃ-kārāspada) is the same— the answer is no.

In the first position, since the ego (ahaṅkāra) is not the locus-determinant (adhiṣṭhāna-avacchedaka) as the mother-of-pearl is [the locus-determinant] for silver, there is no contingency of an error such as "I am an elephant," in the same way that one does not have the error "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl.

This is because the cognition "I" is opposed to error just like the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl," and because it is admitted that the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) appears therein precisely as something not opposed to error.
In the final view, however, just as the form "elephant" is imagined, so too is this form "this" merely imagined.
Even when both forms are sublated, there is no consequence of falling into nihilism (śūnyavāda), because the consciousness that serves as the substrate remains unsublated;
furthermore, even in the waking state, it is admitted that what appears is merely a phenomenal "this-ness" of silver, which is distinct from the "this-ness" of the mother-of-pearl.

For according to the principle stated in *Siddhāntabindu* I.36, "Indeed, it is only that which is superimposed which flashes forth in errors," even in the view that the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) of the mother-of-pearl appears, the reality of the "this-portion" is not the determining factor for superimposition;
rather, it is the reality of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
And in that case, just as the consciousness of the mother-of-pearl is unknown [to the subject], here too the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) certainly exists; this has been established.
Therefore, there is no inconsistency in either of the two positions.
And in this context, the enjoyer of dream-objects is called the Taijasa.
Or rather, it is because its primary nature is the fire called *pitta*, and thus it possesses the power of illumination even without other lights such as the sun;

or because it is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is the place of rest for the individual soul (*jīva*) who has become exhausted by the two types of enjoyment in the waking and dreaming states, when— upon the exhaustion of the karma that causes both of those— the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā*) and delimited by the power of cognition, abides in the form of its cause.
Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the perception of the mere cause [of consciousness], characterized by the thought "I was conscious of nothing.

In that state, although there is an absence of knowledge regarding the objects of experience belonging to the waking and dreaming states, there exists [consciousness] in the form of the witness (*sākṣin*) and in the form of bliss (*sukha*).
Furthermore, it is accepted that ignorance (*avidyā*) has three modes of functioning (*vṛtti*), characterized by the states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] and the forms of cognition.
Moreover, because there is no ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), there is not a single distinct mode of functioning; otherwise, it would follow that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) would be impossible.

For this very reason, since there is an absence of perception in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to the state of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).

Because there is no seed for such a conceptualization in that state, whereas here—in this waking state—the one who has arisen from sleep reflects, "I slept happily; I was not aware of anything"; and because such a reflection would be impossible if there were no prior experience.

Furthermore, because it is not produced by an experience occurring at a time when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is colored [by the object], there is no inconsistency in its being a memory even in the absence of a mention of that [object].

Moreover, since there is no rule that a mention of that [object] must occur in memory, the experience "I slept" during the waking state would otherwise be untenable; and because inference is impossible due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and due to the unestablished nature of its locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is indeed experienced only at the very moment of awakening.
Because [the Self] has dissolved during deep sleep, it is not experienced then, and thus recollection would be impossible;

rather, just as there is the cognition "the face is red" when the redness of a hibiscus flower is superimposed upon the mirror that serves as the locus for the reflection of the face, so too, because the witnessing consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) residing in the ego (ahaṅkāra) is the locus of the recollection, there arises the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya): "I slept."
Furthermore, I do not [identify] with happiness as its substrate;

for memory, doubt, and error are necessarily based on the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) as their substrate, whereas the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is the substrate of knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since its status as an effect is delimited precisely by its being a knower (*pramātṛ*), and since ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is the cause of it when delimited by its being a non-valid cognition (*apramā*), [the ego-sense cannot be the substrate of happiness].

For this very reason, the Vedāntins accept that even indirect error (*parokṣavibhrama*) produced by the words of an unreliable person and so forth is indeed a modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*).

This is because, although the causal complex for generating a mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) may be present there, the internal organ lacks the capacity due to the exclusion of its being a valid cognition (*pramā*).

Furthermore, the superimposition of Brahman upon names and the like is simply a mental modification distinct from both error and valid cognition, as it is dependent on will, just like desire and other such states.
Thus it has been said: "Precisely for this reason, because it is produced by an injunction (*codanā*), that [activity] is indeed a mental action (*mānasī kriyā*) and not knowledge (*jñāna*).
By this, the fact that reasoning (*tarka*) is also a modification of the mind (*manovṛtti*) is explained.
Because that [process], which consists in the implication of the pervader through the imposition of the pervaded, is dependent on volition, it is distinct from both error and valid cognition.

For this very reason, the injunctions such as "it should be heard, it should be reflected upon, it should be meditated upon" are appropriate with respect to the inquiry into the Vedānta known as *śravaṇa*, when accompanied by *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditation),
since that [inquiry] takes the form of reasoning (*tarka*) consisting of the fourfold positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and so forth.
The positive and negative concomitance of the seer and the seen; the positive and negative concomitance of the witness and the witnessed;
and the positive and negative concomitance of that which comes and goes and its limit.

"The positive and negative concomitance [of suffering] with that which is the object of supreme love" refers to the fifth type of positive and negative concomitance, namely, the concomitance between the recurring and the excluded.
The learned authorities maintain that this is an illustration of all the Vedāntic arguments consistent with reason (anukūlatarka) set forth in the four-chaptered Mīmāṃsā.
The detailed account, however, should be sought in the *Vedāntakalpalatikā*.

Thus, in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there exists the enjoyment of bliss, and its enjoyer is called the "wise one" (*prājña*) because he identifies with that state of deep sleep; this is either because of his profound ignorance at that time, or because of his supreme knowledge due to the absence of any limiting distinctions.

At that time, even though the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has dissolved, because it is still delimited by its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is no consequence of the non-existence of the individual soul (*jīva*),
nor does the state of omniscience follow. Furthermore,
the teaching regarding non-difference from the Lord (*īśvara*) is merely figurative, based on the absence of identification with the body, senses, and so forth.

Furthermore, since the *saṃskāra* (mental impression) functions as a non-inherent cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), it does not enter into the category of the material cause (*upādāna*) of the effects residing in the Witness; therefore, even when that [impression] varies, there is no variation in the Witness.

In the waking state, however, because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) enters into the category of the material cause of the effects residing in the means of valid cognition (*pramā*), there is indeed a distinction of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) due to the distinction of that [organ].
And since the status of being a cognizer belongs to the Witness itself as qualified by additional adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no inconsistency regarding the recognition [of objects across states].
Even though there are distinctions in the measure of the mother [and other objects], the witness does not differ with each body;
because it is like an external object [in its uniformity], it is therefore called the Self (ātman).
"Just as the mutual deviation of the knower and so forth is witnessed by their own respective witnesses,
the Self is not like that, because It is the witness of the non-existence of all knowers and so forth.

Since the venerable Vārttikakāra has thus refuted the distinction between witnesses even during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), it should be understood that the postulation of such a distinction by some [others] regarding deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is nothing but delusion.
[Objection: Surely, because some person at some time has the reflective awareness, "I slept in pain," there must also be an experience of pain during deep sleep.

[Reply: No, because at that time there is an absence of such [pain] due to the lack of the causal complex for pain. Furthermore, since pleasure is the very nature of the Self, it is eternal; and when the bed and so forth are unfavorable, it is merely a figurative usage to call it "pain. Thus, the cognition "I slept in pain" is logically established.
Alternatively, since each of the three states is itself accepted as being threefold, suffering is established even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
For instance, valid cognition is "waking-waking" (*jāgraj-jāgrat*),
while an error such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is "waking-dream" (*jāgrat-svapna*).
The state of being paralyzed by fatigue and the like while in the waking state is "waking-sleep.
Likewise, obtaining mantras and so forth in a dream is "dream-waking";
the cognition that "I have seen a dream even within a dream" is "dream-dream."
That which is experienced during the state of dreaming cannot be described while one is in the waking state; that is "dream-sleep.

Likewise, even in the state of deep sleep, that sattvic mental modification (vṛtti) which takes the form of bliss is "waking within deep sleep," followed by the subsequent reflective awareness: "I slept happily."

In that very state, the rajasic modification is dream-sleep; immediately after that, the reflection "I slept poorly" becomes possible. In that same state, the tamasic modification is deep sleep within deep sleep (suṣupti-suṣupti).
Immediately following that, there is the reflective awareness, "I was deeply deluded.
How this is so is clearly explained in the *Vāsiṣṭhavārtikāmṛta* and other such works.
Thus, with respect to the internal self, there is the Viśva state.

Virāṭ is the cosmic being with respect to the objective world (adhibhūta), Viṣṇu is the cosmic being with respect to the divine (adhidaiva), and the waking state is the cosmic being with respect to the self (adhyātma).
With respect to the divine (adhidaiva), it is protection; with respect to the elemental (adhibhūta), it is the quality of sattva.
Thus, with respect to the internal (adhyātma), it is the taijasa state.
Hiraṇyagarbha is with respect to the objective world (adhibhūta), Brahmā is with respect to the divine (adhidaiva),
and dreaming is with respect to the self (adhyātma).
With respect to the divine (adhidaiva), it is creation;
with respect to the elemental (adhibhūta), it is the quality of passion (rajo-guṇa);
and likewise, with respect to the self (adhyātma), it is the conscious one (prājña).
The unmanifest is the objective realm;
Rudra is the divine realm;
deep sleep is the internal realm.
Dissolution is the divine aspect (adhidaiva), and the quality of darkness (tamas) is the elemental aspect (adhibhūta).

Thus, because of the unity of these— namely the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva)— which are accompanied by the three parts of the syllable Om (praṇava), one attains the world of Hiraṇyagarbha through the meditation on their identity.
And there is gradual liberation (kramamukti) by means of the purification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
However, through the knowledge of the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) alone, by the removal of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), liberation occurs directly.

Thus, since the triad of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—along with their three respective states—is of the nature of ignorance (avidyā) and is false due to its being an object of perception (dṛśyatva), the unconditioned, absolute witness called the Fourth (turīya) [is established].
The meaning is "I am this.

Thus, since all conventional arrangements are established through worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), and since from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) no state whatsoever exists, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
This has been explained by us in detail in the *Vedāntakalpalatikā*, so we shall desist here. // 8 //

Now, an objection: since all three states— waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— together with their respective presiding deities, are false, it would follow that even the Witness of those states is false,
as there is no distinction between them.
Anticipating this objection, he declares the truthfulness of the witness by means of specific designations:

"Because of its pervasiveness, because of its application as the Beneficent (Hita), because its existence is self-established, and because it has no other support—this entire world is insubstantial; that which is other than it is the one remaining Śiva, I alone. (9)

Based on the scriptural statement, “One should not see the seer of seeing” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.4.2), which refers to the Witness, and the subsequent statement, “Whatever is other than this is perishable” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.4.2), it follows that everything other than the Witness— the entire world of objects witnessed— is insubstantial, but the Witness itself is not.

The word "api" (also/even) has the sense of a collective inclusion (*samuccaya*) for unstated reasons, such as being the limit of sublation (*bādhāvadhitva*), being known as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of error, and the absence of any cognizer of its sublation; [as it is said]:
"Now, that which is small is mortal" (ChU VII.24.1).

Since the Śruti states this, and because "limitedness" and "insignificance" are co-extensive, the cessation of insignificance follows from the cessation of limitedness; thus he says, "because of its pervasiveness.
This is because, through the teaching that "all this is indeed Brahman" (ChU III.14.1), it is not limited by space or time, as it is the Self of all.
Furthermore, although space and the like are limited by place and time, they are metaphorically designated as "pervasive" due to their relative vastness.

Now, since the Self is eternal because it is all-pervasive and because it is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva), it is neither of the nature of the cessation of suffering nor of the nature of pleasure.

Since pleasure, being impermanent, cannot logically constitute the nature of the eternal Self, one might suspect that liberation—which is of the very nature of the Self—is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha). Anticipating this objection, he says: "No, because of its application as that which is beneficial (hita)."
Beneficiality is the state of being the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
As it is said: "This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this innermost Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8);
and "That which is the Infinite (*bhūman*) is bliss" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23.1).
"This indeed is the supreme bliss" (BAU IV.3.33);
"Consciousness, bliss is Brahman" (BAU III.9.28).
For, according to such scriptural passages, its nature as supreme bliss is taught.

And although that [Brahman] is eternal, there is a figurative designation of its arising and destruction in the world because it is manifested by various mental modifications (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) produced by merit (*dharma*).

Furthermore, for one who is veiled by ignorance, that [Brahman], though not actually attained, appears as if attained through the mere knowledge [of it] via the cessation of ignorance; thus, the engagement of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) with that end is justified.

Since the superimposed phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is of the nature of suffering, has that very [Brahman] as its substrate, Brahman itself is the absence [of the world]; therefore, it possesses the status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being the absence of suffering.
Now, is bliss experienced in liberation or not?
Not the first [alternative], because at that time, due to the absence of the body, senses, and so forth, there is an absence of any manifestor [of that bliss];
for if one were to admit its experience even in the absence of a manifestor, it would follow by the same logic that it is experienced during the state of saṃsāra as well.
Not the second,
because it would follow that it is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha),
since only that which is being known can be a human goal.
If it is argued that this is merely the outburst of those who consider themselves Vaiṣṇavas—just as [the distinction between] sugar and its eater [is made by the ignorant]—we say no;
for he states: "Because its existence is self-established.
The meaning is: because its nature is self-luminous knowledge.
Although in the state of saṃsāra the Self does not manifest as the nature of supreme bliss because its form is veiled by ignorance, nevertheless,

upon the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), it manifests by itself as the nature of supreme bliss through its own self-luminosity; thus, there is no dependence on a manifestor.
Now, even if pleasure were of the nature of self-luminous knowledge, it could not be of the nature of the Self;
for knowledge, being the meaning of a verbal root, is an action and thus possesses a substratum, as evidenced by the cognition "I know," and because there is no such cognition as "I am knowledge."
And so, having raised the doubt as to how there can be a doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*), he says "no," for the reason that [the Self] has no other support:
"That Brahman which is immediate and direct, which is the Self within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).
Based on such scriptural passages as these, the Self is indeed of the nature of self-luminous knowledge and bliss.

Due to the superimposition of identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and because of the superimposition of knowledge upon its modification (*vṛtti*), there arises the cognition "I know," which is the perception of [knowledge] having that [internal organ] as its locus.

Since the status of being the meaning of the verbal root and the possession of origination and destruction belong to the modification of the internal organ, and since knowledge in its essential form as pure consciousness (*jñapti*)—being the substratum of all things—has no other locus, there is no possibility of duality.
Therefore, it is established that the Self, whose nature consists of knowledge and bliss, is real, and the entire world, which is distinct from it, is unreal. // 9 //
Now, if the entire world were insubstantial (*tuccha*), the realization of the reality of the Self could not occur through its negation;
for it is a logical principle that what is negated must have been cognized somewhere previously, just as a rabbit’s horn is never negated because it has never been established anywhere.

And thus, since the very impossibility of negation precludes the unreality of the world, [the opponent objects]: "No," he says— "It is not one, nor is there a second other than it; how could there be? It is neither absolute isolation nor non-isolation; it is neither void nor non-void, because of its non-duality. How can I speak of that which is established by all the Vedāntas? (10)
That which possesses the number one is "one.
That which possesses the number two, produced by a relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) directed toward that [first], is "the second.
Therefore, in the absence of the first, how could there be a second?
And the second [term] is also an elliptical indicator for the third and subsequent [terms].
Now, it may be objected: by the scriptural text, “One only, without a second” (ChU VI.2.1), unity is established.
"No," he says—"nor is there isolation. Isolation means oneness;
that [oneness] is due to ignorance (avidyā).
If it is argued that, should the oneness of the Self not be established by scripture,
then its manifoldness would follow from the force of means of valid cognition such as perception, [the author] says "no," stating: "And there is no non-absolute [oneness]."
Non-absolute-ness is multiplicity,
as in: "There is not anything here that is manifold" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.4.19) and "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.2.1).
[This is known] from such scriptural passages as, "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad II.3.6).
If it is argued that, because of the negation of everything, there must be only emptiness, we say: no.
Thus he says: "It is not empty," quoting:
"If one knows Brahman as non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent; but if one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad II.6).
Having begun with, “Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite” (TU II.1) and “In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone” (ChU VI.2.1), [the text concludes]:
“All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That thou art” (ChU VI.8.7).
One might argue that, according to such scriptural passages, [Brahman] would possess attributes such as reality and knowledge;
however, he says "and not non-empty" to refute this.

For even though all distinctions are negated by the two words "one" and "without a second," the particle *eva* (alone/only) further negates distinctions such as the relationship between attribute and substrate, as well as difference and non-difference.
He states the reason for this in all cases: "because of being non-dual" (*advaitakatvāt*).

That which has gone in two ways (*dvidhā itam*) is *dvīta*; the state of that is *dvaita*. As it is said in the *Vārttika*: "They say that what has gone in two ways is *dvīta*; the state of that is called *dvaita*" (BAUBhV IV.3.1807).
The literal meaning of the term *advaita* is that wherein no duality—that is, no state of being divided—exists.
This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "He saw the non-dual, as one [with] water" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.3.32).

The point is that since the cognition of an absence has, by its very nature, the cognition of the counter-positive as its cause, the negation of duality is logically established; for by accepting that duality is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), it is nonetheless perceivable through perception and other means of knowledge.

"In that case, let such a Self be pointed out by means of a gesture with the finger. He says, "No," and explains: "How can I speak?"—this is an objection; for, due to its non-duality, it is beyond the scope of speech.
“He spoke by means of non-speaking” (Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya Upaniṣad VII);
“From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad II.4);
“One should not seek to know the knower by means of cognition” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad III.4.2).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
If it is asked, "If [the Self] is beyond the scope of speech, how can the Vedāntas possess authority regarding it?", the answer is no;

for even though the Self is not an object [of words], they remove its ignorance merely by producing a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of that [Self]. Thus he says: "established by all the Vedāntas."
And so says the Śruti: “He by whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he who thinks he knows it, does not know it.
It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know. (KU II.3) “That which the mind does not think, that by which they say the mind is thought...”
"Know that very Brahman to be yourself; this which they worship is not it" (KU I.5).
Such passages demonstrate that the Self is not an object [of cognition].

Thus, when ignorance is removed by the non-dual mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the Vedānta texts, and all misfortunes imagined by that ignorance are likewise removed, one becomes fulfilled, being of the nature of supreme bliss. This is established.
I do not praise that Vyāsa who did not properly bind the entire meaning even with his aphorisms;
rather, I praise Śaṅkara and Sureśvara, by whom the whole meaning was composed even without those [sūtras]. // 1 //
Though brief, this treatise, like a wish-fulfilling gem, brings forth manifold meanings;
it has been composed by the virtuous sage Madhusūdana for the delight of those possessed of merit.
Whatever excellence there is herein belongs to my guru as much as it does to me; whatever lack of excellence there is herein belongs to me alone and not to my guru. (3)
Through much entreaty, I have made this brief compendium for Balabhadra.
Whatever herein is faultless and whatever is faulty, may the noble and wise discern it. (4)
Thus ends the work titled *Siddhāntabindu*, composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
